To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is a polynomial-time approximation scheme for finding the minimum number of questions to ask, (2) the problem is NP-hard to find the minimum number of queries to ask, and (3) the number of queries required to find a target is at most the diameter of the graph plus the depth of the target in the graph.

1) the problem of optimizing the number of questions is NP-complete, 2) there are polynomial-time approximation algorithms for optimizing the number of nodes visited, 3) the number of questions asked by our approximation algorithms is provably bounded by the number of questions required by the optimal solution, and 4) our approximation algorithms perform well on real data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question “How can we best utilize human computation to search a graph?”
the design of algorithms for optimizing human-assisted graph searches.
the design of algorithms to optimize the use of humans in graph search, which has applications in many real domains.
